title: Iterator Ownership and Laziness
concept: Borrowing iteration, consuming iteration and deliberate collection

writing.summary: An iterator pipeline describes work; the item type and terminal operation determine ownership and execution.
writing.explanation:
For a `Vec<T>`, `iter` normally yields `&T`, `iter_mut` yields `&mut T` and `into_iter` on an owned vector yields `T`. The chosen receiver matters: `into_iter` on a reference can still borrow. Read the actual item type before deciding whether an operation moves, copies or clones values.

Most iterator adapters are lazy. `map` describes a transformation, while a consumer such as `collect` or `sum` drives it. Returning an iterator can avoid collecting an intermediate vector, but keeps any captured input borrows alive for the returned iterator’s lifetime. Calling `cloned` on an iterator of references requests `Clone` on its items; it is not a free conversion for every `T`.

The example computes lengths by borrowing the strings and then proves the original vector remains usable. A second pipeline consumes it into another collection. Explain both the data flow and when work occurs. In an interview, follow up by returning an `impl Iterator<Item = &str>` tied to the input. That exposes lifetime reasoning more clearly than naming adapter methods from memory.
writing.exampleCaption: Borrowing iteration preserves the input; owned `into_iter` consumes this vector.
writing.rule: Trace the receiver, iterator item type and consumer before making a move or allocation claim.
writing.task: Explain the example, predict the result, and justify your answer to the follow-up.
writing.success: Identify the relevant ownership or API contract and test the changed constraint.
writing.question: Why can `words` still be read after collecting these lengths?
answers: collect implicitly clones every String in the source vector.
iter yields shared references and the map produces lengths without moving strings.
Every iterator pipeline automatically returns ownership to its original container.
writing.feedback: The pipeline borrows `&String` values and collects `usize` results. A consuming receiver or a different adapter can change the ownership contract.

recall.question: For `v: Vec<String>`, what item types do `v.iter()`, `v.iter_mut()`, `v.into_iter()` and `(&v).into_iter()` yield?
recall.answer: `&String`, `&mut String`, `String` and `&String`. Only `into_iter` on the owned vector consumes `v`; called on a reference, `into_iter` still just borrows.

recall.question: In what order does this code print, and why?
recall.answer: `built` first, then `visit 1`, `visit 2`, `visit 3`, then `12`. `map` is lazy and only describes the work; the `sum` consumer drives the iterator.

depth.misconception: Every iterator pipeline automatically returns ownership to its original container.
depth.correction: Nothing is returned, because nothing left. `iter` only lends references; `into_iter` on an owned `Vec` consumes it and never gives it back.
